title: 05 — Agents and Multi-Agent Systems
html:
05 — Agents and Multi-Agent Systems

The one idea: an agent is a loop: the model decides the next step, your code runs the tool, and the result goes back, until the task is done. Build one only when the steps can't be fixed in advance. Give it few, well-made tools, a budget, and a person in front of anything irreversible.

1. What it is

Tier Who decides the steps Use when
Single call Nobody: one prompt, one answer Classify, extract, summarise
Workflow Your code: fixed steps, each maybe a model call The steps are known (extract, then validate, then file)
Agent The model: chooses tools and order at run time Open-ended tasks that are hard to specify step by step
Multi-agent Several agents with roles, or a lead with helpers Work that fans out (research many sources) or needs separation of duties

Before building an agent, check four things:

  1. Is the task genuinely multi-step and hard to specify?
  2. Is the outcome worth the extra cost and latency?
  3. Can the model do this kind of task well?
  4. Can errors be caught and recovered?

If any answer is no, use a workflow.

2. Why it matters

  • Agents are the most capable and most expensive pattern, and the easiest to make unsafe.
  • Most failures are tool design (vague tools, too many tools), missing budgets, and no human checkpoint, not model quality.

3. The main ideas

3.1 The loop

---
title: The agent loop with guards
---
flowchart TD
    T["Task"] --> C["Call model with tools"]
    C --> D{"Stop reason?"}
    D -- "answer" --> DONE["Return answer"]
    D -- "tool calls" --> G{"Side effect?"}
    G -- "yes" --> H["Ask a person"]
    G -- "no" --> R["Run tools (in parallel)"]
    H --> R
    R --> B{"Within step and<br/>token budget?"}
    B -- "yes" --> C
    B -- "no" --> STOP["Stop and report progress"]

3.2 Ways to build one

Approach What you get Notes (checked 2026-10-27)
Your own loop on a model API Full control 20 to 50 lines. See the code in section 4
SDK tool runner (for example the Anthropic SDK's tool_runner) The loop for tools you define, with hooks for approval and logging You host it. 02 has the code
Claude Agent SDK The Claude Code harness as a library: file, shell and search tools, subagents, hooks, permissions You host it. Docs at code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk
Claude Managed Agents (beta) Anthropic runs the loop and a per-session sandbox. Versioned agent configs, scheduling, multi-agent workflows Platform availability varies. Check the docs
Microsoft Agent Framework (.NET and Python) Agents and multi-agent orchestration on top of Microsoft.Extensions.AI. It is the successor to Semantic Kernel and AutoGen Version 1.0 went GA in April 2026 (sources differ by days). Semantic Kernel and AutoGen are in maintenance
LangGraph, OpenAI Agents SDK, Google ADK, CrewAI and others Graph or role-based orchestration Compare on tracing, state handling, human-in-the-loop support and your language

3.3 Tools, memory and context

  • Fewer, better tools. Each tool is a contract (04). If there are dozens, use tool search or group them by skill.
  • Context fills up. Clear old tool results, summarise, or hand reading-heavy subtasks to a sub-agent that returns only a short result.
  • Memory: scoped per user or task, tagged with its source, with an expiry. Never let one user's memory reach another.
  • Budgets: a maximum number of steps, a token or cost budget, and a wall-clock timeout.

3.4 Multi-agent patterns

Pattern Shape Use
Orchestrator and workers A lead plans and delegates to cheaper workers, then merges Research across many sources, per-document work
Pipeline Agent A's output feeds agent B Draft, then review
Maker and checker One proposes, another verifies against criteria Quality-critical outputs

Agent-to-agent interoperability: the A2A protocol (Agent2Agent) standardises how agents discover each other (through an Agent Card, JSON metadata) and hand off tasks. Per one explainer it has reached v1.0. It joined MCP under the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation in August 2026. MCP connects an agent to tools and data, and A2A connects agents to agents.

4. Working code

The script runs the agent loop with a scripted stand-in model, so it is deterministic and offline. It makes two parallel tool calls in one step, holds a side-effect tool (email) for human approval, and enforces a step limit. Standard library only.

import json

# The agent loop every framework runs: call the model, run any tools it asks for, send results back,
# repeat until it answers, with a step limit and an approval gate. The "model" is scripted so this runs
# offline; it returns the same shapes a real tool-using model returns.
SCRIPT = [
    {"stop_reason": "tool_use", "calls": [{"id": "c1", "name": "get_nav", "input": {"isin": "INF000X01AB1", "date": "2026-10-22"}},
                                          {"id": "c2", "name": "get_nav", "input": {"isin": "INF000X01AB1", "date": "2026-10-23"}}]},
    {"stop_reason": "tool_use", "calls": [{"id": "c3", "name": "send_email", "input": {"to": "client@example.com", "body": "NAV rose 0.53%"}}]},
    {"stop_reason": "end_turn", "text": "NAV rose from 142.10 to 142.85 (+0.53%). The email needs your approval before it is sent."},
]
NAV = {"2026-10-22": 142.10, "2026-10-23": 142.85}
TOOLS = {
    "get_nav":    {"side_effect": False, "fn": lambda a: {"nav": NAV[a["date"]]}},
    "send_email": {"side_effect": True,  "fn": lambda a: {"sent": True}},
}

def run_agent(task, approve=lambda call: False, max_steps=5):
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": task}]
    for step, reply in enumerate(SCRIPT[:max_steps], start=1):
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": reply})
        if reply["stop_reason"] == "end_turn":
            return reply["text"], step, messages
        results = []
        for call in reply["calls"]:                       # parallel calls -> all results in ONE message
            tool = TOOLS[call["name"]]
            if tool["side_effect"] and not approve(call):
                results.append({"tool_use_id": call["id"], "is_error": True,
                                "content": "Not run: needs human approval."})
                continue
            results.append({"tool_use_id": call["id"], "content": json.dumps(tool["fn"](call["input"]))})
        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})
        print(f"step {step}: ran {[c['name'] for c in reply['calls']]} -> {[r['content'] for r in results]}")
    return "Stopped: step limit reached.", max_steps, messages

answer, steps, transcript = run_agent("How did plan INF000X01AB1 move yesterday? Email the client.")
print(f"answer after {steps} model calls: {answer}")
print("messages in transcript:", len(transcript))
print("with max_steps=1:", run_agent("same task", max_steps=1)[0])

Output:

step 1: ran ['get_nav', 'get_nav'] -> ['{"nav": 142.1}', '{"nav": 142.85}']
step 2: ran ['send_email'] -> ['Not run: needs human approval.']
answer after 3 model calls: NAV rose from 142.10 to 142.85 (+0.53%). The email needs your approval before it is sent.
messages in transcript: 6
step 1: ran ['get_nav', 'get_nav'] -> ['{"nav": 142.1}', '{"nav": 142.85}']
with max_steps=1: Stopped: step limit reached.

What to notice:

  • Two get_nav calls in one model turn have their results returned together in one message. Splitting them across messages teaches models to stop calling tools in parallel.
  • send_email is not executed. It returns an error result saying it needs approval, and the model's final answer says so honestly.
  • With max_steps=1, the agent stops and reports, instead of running away.

5. Common mistakes

  1. An agent where a workflow would do. It is slower, costlier and less predictable.
  2. Too many overlapping tools. The model picks the wrong one.
  3. No budgets. Loops run up cost.
  4. Irreversible actions without a person.
  5. No tracing. You can't debug what you can't see (08).

6. Exercise (2 hours)

  1. Add a token budget to the script: stop when a running total of (made-up) tokens exceeds a limit.
  2. Add an approve function that approves only emails to @example.com addresses, and test both paths.
  3. Rebuild it with an SDK tool runner against a real model, and compare the transcripts.

7. Questions to test yourself

  1. When should you use a workflow instead of an agent?
  2. What three budgets should every agent have?
  3. Why return all parallel tool results in one message?
  4. What is the difference between MCP and A2A?
  5. What replaced Semantic Kernel and AutoGen for new .NET agent work?

Answers

  1. When the steps are known in advance, or the cost of an error is high and hard to recover from.
  2. A step limit, a token or cost budget, and a time limit.
  3. It is the expected shape, and splitting results discourages parallel calls in later turns.
  4. MCP connects an agent to tools and data. A2A connects agents to other agents.
  5. Microsoft Agent Framework (version 1.0, GA in 2026).
